pr_title: module-util: use the blacklist from module_blacklist= in cmdline
pr_body:
When a module is blacklisted using `module_blacklist=`, we shouldn't fail with 'Operation not permitted'. Instead we check for it and skip it if this is the case. (Detailed reasons  in #25182)

Closes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/25182
pr_comments:
> When a module is blacklisted using `module_blacklist=`, we shouldn't fail with 'Operation not permitted'.

"We" do not fail anything. The error is returned by kernel. "We" should not be holier than the pope.

> the kernel command line should be handled by kmod

The kernel command line should be handled by kernel, not by kmod and not by systemd. `module_blacklist=` is **kernel** parameter. The non-issue "fixed" here is the result of misunderstanding what  modprobe blacklist actually does and confusion based on name similarity. 

Silently ignoring to load module that is explicitly requested to be loaded is wrong.

> "We" do not fail anything. The error is returned by kernel. "We" should not be holier than the pope.

In this case we can be sure that **the user** is using a kernel parameter to blacklist kernel modules. We should respect what they do.

This causes a significant performance regression (at least from what I've noticed in TEST-64-UDEV-STORAGE after running it a couple of times against this PR and the main branch), e.g.:

```
test                     this PR     main
-----------------------------------------
testcase_btrfs_basic     287s        30s
testcase_iscsi_lvm       207s        26s
testcase_long_sysfs_path 52s         14s
testcase_lvm_basic       358s        122s
...
```

issue_context.title: modules-load: should not fail when `module_blacklist` is used to blacklist modules
issue_context.body:
Currently, `systemd-modules-load.service` fails when `module_blacklist=` is used to block a module from being loaded, while `modprobe.blacklist` allows it to start successfully. I think for both cases, `modules-load` should exit normally as the user is explicitly blacklisting those modules.

I know that `kmod` is responsible for the actual module loading. But in this specific case, I believe systemd should take care of this. Since `kmod` is usually used to manually load modules, and the kernel would still block it eventually, it's not that necessary for them to check kernel cmdline for this. However, what `systemd-modules-load` does is to autoload these modules in the boot process, and thus makes being aware of both of the blacklisting methods matter.
comments:
> Currently, `systemd-modules-load.service` fails when `module_blacklist=` is used to block a module from being loaded, while `modprobe.blacklist` allows it to start successfully.

These two parameters have completely different semantic, are interpreted by different components and `modprobe.blacklist` is not related to `systemd-modules-load.service` in any way (the former is applied when resolving module alias while the latter explicitly loads module under its final canonical name).

> `modules-load` should exit normally as the user is explicitly blacklisting those modules

If you do not want the module to be loaded, do not force load it using `systemd-modules-load.service`. If you **do** want module to be loaded and it failed to load (for whatever reason) it certainly sounds wrong to silently ignore it.

`module_blacklist=` is kernel parameter that absolutely prohibits the specified modules to be loaded. There is no reason to use it unless you are debugging something at which point "failure" of `systemd-modules-load.service` is the least concern. If you want to permanently stop module from being loaded, remove it from `modules-load.d` after having booted once with `modules_blacklist=`.

> These two parameters have completely different semantic, are interpreted by different components and modprobe.blacklist is not related to systemd-modules-load.service in any way (the former is applied when resolving module alias while the latter explicitly loads module under its final canonical name).

I've mentioned my reasons towards whether systemd or kmod should handle this.

> If you do not want the module to be loaded, do not force load it using systemd-modules-load.service. If you do want module to be loaded and it failed to load (for whatever reason) it certainly sounds wrong to silently ignore it.

But by using `modprobe.blacklist`, it's doing what you call "wrong" (kmod silently ignores it, and modules-load exits normally). The loading strategy towards both methods of blacklisting should align.

> module_blacklist= is kernel parameter that absolutely prohibits the specified modules to be loaded. There is no reason to use it unless you are debugging something at which point "failure" of systemd-modules-load.service is the least concern. If you want to permanently stop module from being loaded, remove it from modules-load.d after having booted once with modules_blacklist=.

Sometimes the upstream/distro packaging would ship a `modules-load` conf that autoloads certain modules, and I want to prohibit it from loading in all possible ways. Based on my statement above, `modprobe.blacklist` can actually block it from loading automatically and make `modules-load` exit normally, with or without reconfiguring `modules-load`.


Anyways, if I use `modprobe.blacklist` together with `module_blacklist`, it would produce the desired behavior i.e. `modules-load` exits successfully and the module is blacklisted both manually and automatically. My idea is simply that I should only need one of them to blacklist loading without interfering `modules-load`.

review_comments: Please break lines in the commit message.
